Chapter 2: The Core Principle—Less, But Better.
So, once you’ve realized how easy it is to get overcommitted, what’s the next step? It comes down to embracing a new way of thinking: focus on less, but do it better.
This idea—essentialism—is all about making intentional choices, instead of just letting life push you along on autopilot. It’s a mindset, a discipline, where you pursue what’s truly important and consciously say no to the rest.
Here’s the thing: essentialism isn’t about getting more done. It’s about making sure you get the right things done. Imagine it as a system that helps you figure out where you can make the biggest difference—and then, pouring your energy and resources into those few, vital areas. It means accepting that you can’t do everything. Every time you choose to focus on one thing, you’re choosing not to focus on something else.
Let’s picture this with a simple image. Think about a lamp. If you focus its beam, it can cut through the darkness and light up what matters. But if that light is scattered, it barely makes a dent. Essentialism is about narrowing that beam—directing your attention and your effort to where it counts the most.
And this principle isn’t just for work. In business, it might mean focusing on a couple of key projects, instead of spreading yourself thin across too many. If you’re a leader, it could be about setting clear priorities for your team and shielding them from distractions. In your personal life, it’s choosing a few meaningful relationships or activities, rather than trying to keep up with dozens of shallow connections.
The essentialist mindset is built on a few simple beliefs.
First—almost everything is noise. Only a handful of things are truly valuable.
Second—saying no isn’t about rejecting people. It’s about staying true to what matters most.
Third—clarity about your purpose and your priorities is the foundation for real progress.
And finally, you need boundaries to protect your time and energy for those vital few things.
Adopting this mindset means switching the question you ask yourself. Instead of, “How can I fit it all in?” try asking, “What’s the most important thing I can do right now?” It’s about moving from chasing after every external demand, to being guided by your own clear sense of what matters.
Here’s a practical example. Picture a manager who’s swamped with too many projects. Instead of trying to juggle them all, she decides to pinpoint the one initiative that would make the biggest difference for her company. She rallies the team around this goal, and suddenly, results improve—and morale goes up. The secret isn’t working harder. It’s working smarter. Choosing less, but making it count.
Essentialism isn’t a one-and-done decision. It’s a habit—a process of constantly checking in, asking yourself, “Is this really the best use of my time and energy?” and being willing to let go of the rest.
Over time, this discipline adds up. You’ll see greater impact. More satisfaction. And, maybe best of all, a real sense of peace of mind.
